scenario: A SQL Server 2019 estate relies on a dozen SQL Agent jobs, a linked server to a warehouse system and cross-database joins with three-part names. The team wants Microsoft to own OS and engine patching and has eight weeks to move.
stem: Which Azure SQL flavour is the honest first choice?
options: Azure SQL Database, rewriting the Agent jobs as Functions and the cross-database joins as Elastic Query
Azure SQL Managed Instance, because it keeps Agent, linked servers and cross-database queries while Microsoft runs the engine
SQL Server on an Azure VM, because only IaaS supports SQL Agent
Azure SQL Database in an elastic pool, since pooled databases can query each other directly
explanation: Managed Instance exists precisely for instance-shaped estates: Agent, linked servers and cross-database queries all work, and Microsoft still patches the engine and OS. The SQL Database route is possible but stacks three workarounds into an eight-week window; the VM answer is wrong because Managed Instance also has Agent, and pooling changes billing, not the T-SQL surface.

stem: Why does Microsoft steer new workloads to the vCore purchasing model rather than DTU?
options: DTU databases cannot be backed up automatically
vCore prices compute, memory and storage separately, and supports Azure Hybrid Benefit and reservations
vCore databases are always cheaper than DTU databases at every size
DTU is only available on Managed Instance and SQL Server VMs
explanation: vCore makes the bill legible - you can see and change compute, memory and storage independently - and it is where Hybrid Benefit and reservations apply. DTU is not always dearer; a 5-DTU Basic database is about $5 a month, cheaper than anything on vCore, which is exactly why the 'always cheaper' option is a trap.

scenario: A developer creates the dev copy of the orders database on Business Critical 'so it matches production', and finance queries a database line costing three times what they expected.
options: Move dev to the General Purpose tier, ideally serverless with auto-pause, since local SSD and replicas buy nothing for a dev workload
Keep Business Critical but turn off zone redundancy to bring the price down
Move dev to Hyperscale, which is the cheapest vCore tier
Keep Business Critical and apply a reservation, which removes most of the premium
explanation: Business Critical costs roughly 2.5-3x General Purpose because of local SSD and a three-replica cluster, none of which a dev database uses; serverless General Purpose bills per vCore-second and pauses to storage-only when idle. Hyperscale is a size-and-restore tier, not a bargain tier, and a reservation discounts a commitment rather than removing the Business Critical premium.

scenario: An internal reporting tool on a serverless Azure SQL Database fails its first query every morning with a connection error, then works normally for the rest of the day.
stem: What is happening and what is the right response?
options: The firewall rule expires overnight; add a permanent IP rule
The database auto-paused after an hour idle and takes about a minute to resume; the app needs retry logic, or a longer auto-pause delay if the cost is acceptable
Serverless databases lose their connection pool at midnight; restart the app service nightly
The database failed over to its geo-secondary overnight; repoint the connection string
explanation: Auto-pause is the point of serverless - you pay storage only while paused - and the resume takes around a minute, during which connections fail with a transient error. Retry with back-off fixes it properly; a longer auto-pause delay trades money for convenience. Firewall rules do not expire and geo-failover would not resolve itself an hour later.

stem: How does a failover group differ from active geo-replication on its own?
options: A failover group replicates synchronously, so no data is lost on failover
A failover group works only with Managed Instance, while geo-replication works only with SQL Database
A failover group adds a listener DNS name and fails a set of databases over together, automatically after a grace period, so connection strings do not change
A failover group replicates to any region, while geo-replication is limited to the region pair
explanation: Both use asynchronous replication; the group adds the listener name, group-level failover and an automatic trigger, which is what stops a failover from becoming a connection-string hunt. The synchronous option is the tempting wrong answer - a forced failover can still lose the last seconds of commits, so RPO is seconds rather than zero.

scenario: A code review finds the Node API's connection string in an app setting with a SQL login and password embedded in it.
options: Rotate the SQL password monthly and keep it in the app setting
Connect with the app's managed identity through Entra ID authentication and switch the server to Entra-only, so there is no password at all
Move the SQL password into Key Vault and read it through a managed identity
Turn on transparent data encryption so the connection string is encrypted at rest
explanation: Entra ID authentication with a managed identity removes the secret rather than hiding it, and Entra-only mode stops anyone recreating a SQL login later. Putting the password in Key Vault is better than an app setting but still leaves a password to rotate and leak; TDE encrypts data files on disk and has nothing to do with connection strings.

scenario: Six weeks after go-live, finance asks for the orders database as it stood on a date five weeks ago. The team has changed nothing about backups since creating the database.
options: Automatic backups are kept for a year, so the restore is a portal click
Point-in-time restore keeps only about seven days by default, and long-term retention was never configured, so that date is gone
Backups only exist if a Recovery Services vault was attached, so there are no backups at all
Business Critical keeps 35 days automatically, so it depends on the tier chosen
explanation: Azure SQL takes backups automatically from day one, but the default point-in-time window is seven days (configurable up to 35) and long-term retention is off until someone sets a policy. The vault answer is wrong because SQL PaaS backups do not need one, and no tier extends retention by itself.

scenario: A checkout API on an S0 database slows to a crawl on Saturday afternoons; the portal shows DTU at 100% but the team cannot tell whether CPU or I/O is the problem.
stem: What is the most useful next step?
options: Add indexes until the DTU metric drops, since 100% DTU always means missing indexes
Move the database to the vCore model on General Purpose, where CPU, memory and I/O are visible and sized separately, and check the connection pool against the worker limit
Enable read scale-out on the S0 database so reads go to a replica
Put the database into an elastic pool with the reporting database to borrow its unused DTUs
explanation: DTU bundles the three resources into one opaque number, which is exactly why the team cannot diagnose it; vCore separates them and gives a clearer worker and tempdb ceiling to check the Node pool against. Indexes may help but cannot be assumed from a saturated DTU meter, read scale-out needs Business Critical or Hyperscale, and pooling with one other database rarely covers a shared Saturday peak.
